before.label: Structural linguistics
before.description: Signs acquire value through relations and differences within systems. Structural linguistics offers a model that travels into anthropology, literary analysis, and psychoanalysis.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Saussure’s Course in General Linguistics (1916, posthumous); Roman Jakobson is an important intermediary for Lévi-Strauss.

representative_people.context: A named resource in Lévi-Strauss’s phonological analogy; the chapter warns against literal transfer to kinship.
representative_people.works: “Principien der historischen Phonologie” (1931); “Observations sur le classement phonologique des consonnes” (1938); Kindersprache, Aphasie und allgemeine Lautgesetze (1941), cited in Structural Anthropology

before.scope_note: Saussure’s relational signs and Jakobson’s mediation are different stages; do not treat every structuralist as a direct pupil.

after.label: Structural linguistics
after.date_label: Saussure and later linguistic programmes · twentieth century
after.description: Relational signs, language states and historical change, phonological analysis, and social uses of language form distinct inquiries. Later semiology, anthropology, psychoanalysis and historical debates adapt and criticize particular concepts.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Saussure’s Course in General Linguistics (1916, posthumous); Roman Jakobson is an important intermediary for Lévi-Strauss.

representative_people.context: Relational value, social convention and distinct analyses of language states and change. The posthumous Course is an editorial reconstruction of teaching, not a finished authorial manuscript.
representative_people.works: Cours de linguistique générale (1916; consulted 1971 edition), Parts I–II

representative_people.context: A named resource in Lévi-Strauss’s phonological analogy; the chapter warns against literal transfer to kinship. His analysis of selection and combination also differentiates metaphoric and metonymic operations.
representative_people.works: “Principien der historischen Phonologie” (1931); “Observations sur le classement phonologique des consonnes” (1938); Kindersprache, Aphasie und allgemeine Lautgesetze (1941), cited in Structural Anthropology; “Two Aspects of Language and Two Types of Aphasic Disturbances” (selected reprint, pp. 95–114)

representative_people.context: Coeditor who helped reconstruct the Course from teaching materials and acknowledged editorial responsibility.
representative_people.works: Editorial preparation and first-edition preface of Cours de linguistique générale (1916)

representative_people.context: Coeditor credited in the preface with collating third-course notebooks; editorial arrangement mediates the published argument.
representative_people.works: Editorial preparation and first-edition preface of Cours de linguistique générale (1916)

representative_people.context: Student and collaborator whose notebooks and collation of the first two courses contributed to the posthumous book.
representative_people.works: Editorial preparation and first-edition preface of Cours de linguistique générale (1916)

representative_people.context: A distinct social and historical approach: changes in word meaning are related to group practices and circulation between vocabularies. This selection does not equate his programme with autonomous structural analysis.

Phonological relations provide a named resource in Lévi-Strauss’s methodological analogy, whose limits are explicit. Selection is supported by that reception, not a full review of Trubetzkoy’s corpus.
representative_people.works: “La phonologie actuelle” (1933), cited and discussed in Structural Anthropology

representative_people.context: Reworks langue/parole through schema, norm and usage; Barthes explicitly discusses this reformulation. His formal programme is distinct from Meillet’s social explanation.
representative_people.works: “Langue et parole,” Cahiers Ferdinand de Saussure 2 (issue dated 1942; bibliography lists 1943), 29–44

representative_people.context: A retrospective historical recipient who discusses relational signs, the linguistic turn and contested reference. Her later address is bibliography about the mapped period, not an extension of coverage.

after.scope_note: A selective teaching umbrella, not one uniform school or a claim that all linguistics descends from Saussure. The Course is posthumously reconstructed; Meillet’s social explanation, phonological programmes and Hjelmslev’s formal distinctions differ. Later reception is separately evidenced. Benveniste and broader linguistic traditions remain review gaps.

strands.title: Teaching, notebooks and editorial reconstruction
strands.focus: The 1916 book joins material from three courses; its editors describe collation and reconstruction. Published order should not be confused with a single delivered course.

strands.title: Signs, convention and relational value
strands.focus: A sign joins signifier and signified; its value also depends on relations to other signs. Arbitrariness does not mean unrestricted individual choice.
strands.works: Course, Part I chapter I and Part II chapter IV

strands.title: Language states and historical change
strands.focus: Synchrony and diachrony distinguish analytical questions. Social inheritance and change remain part of the Course’s account; structural inquiry is not simply absence of history.

strands.title: Social groups and changing meanings
strands.focus: Meillet asks how vocabularies change within and between groups, explicitly drawing on Durkheim. This is a distinct causal inquiry rather than a synonym for relational value.

strands.title: Phonological relations and methodological transfer
strands.focus: Trubetzkoy and Jakobson are named resources in Lévi-Strauss’s analogy; transferring phonological models to kinship requires qualification.
strands.works: “La phonologie actuelle” (1933); Jakobson’s 1931/1938 works as cited in Structural Anthropology

strands.title: Schema, norm and usage
strands.focus: Hjelmslev’s reformulation distinguishes pure form from norms, habits and acts; the teaching account here follows Barthes’s explicit exposition.
strands.works: “Langue et parole” (1942/1943); Elements of Semiology, I.1.5

strands.title: Selection, combination and discourse
strands.focus: Jakobson differentiates similarity and contiguity, then metaphor and metonymy. These analytical distinctions are not a universal key to every historical text.
strands.works: “Two Aspects of Language,” sections II and V

strands.title: Adaptation, criticism and historical reception
strands.focus: Barthes proposes a revised semiology; Derrida questions speech/writing assumptions; Spiegel retrospectively discusses historical debates. These are distinct interventions.
strands.works: Elements of Semiology (1964); De la grammatologie (1967); “The Task of the Historian” (2009, retrospective)

before.label: Social facts & collective life
before.description: Social facts, division of labour, solidarity, and collective representations. Provides resources for studying social structures and collective ways of thinking.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Émile Durkheim (1858–1917), The Division of Labour in Society (1893); influence on Bloch is substantial but selective and critical.

representative_people.context: Sociological resource; later historical uses are selective.
representative_people.works: The Division of Labour in Society (1893)

before.scope_note: Collective life, classification, and historical comparison are selectively adapted; influence does not mean doctrinal agreement.

after.label: Social facts & collective life
after.description: Social facts, causes and functions, solidarity, ritual and collective thought provide distinct sociological questions. Hubert, Mauss, Simiand, Halbwachs and Meillet develop particular inquiries; historical and anthropological recipients adapt them selectively.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Émile Durkheim (1858–1917), The Division of Labour in Society (1893); influence on Bloch is substantial but selective and critical.

representative_people.context: Defines a sociological object, distinguishes causes from functions, and investigates conditions of solidarity and collective thought. His arguments and ethnographic assumptions require separate assessment.
representative_people.works: De la division du travail social (1893); Les Règles de la méthode sociologique (1895); Les Formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse (1912)

representative_people.context: Collaborative research on sacrifice and later work on gifts examine ritual relations and obligations; the two projects are not interchangeable.
representative_people.works: With Henri Hubert, “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899); “Essai sur le don” (1925)

representative_people.context: Coauthors a provisional comparative theory of sacrifice that distinguishes participants, consecration and mediation. His contribution is not absorbed into Mauss’s later gift essay.
representative_people.works: With Marcel Mauss, “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899)

representative_people.context: Pursues the methodological relation between historical evidence and social science. Annales explicitly reprints his intervention in 1960 as part of its continuing dialogue.
representative_people.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903; Annales reprint, 1960)

representative_people.context: Develops the social frameworks of remembering as a distinct inquiry. Later critical reuse and his intellectual formation are separate evidentiary questions.
representative_people.works: Les Cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); On Collective Memory (edited English collection, 1992)

representative_people.context: Explicitly applies Durkheim’s social-fact definition to language and investigates social conditions of semantic change.
A selective historical recipient and interlocutor, not a doctrinal adherent. His acknowledgment of Durkheim is documented in the scholarly introduction cited here.
representative_people.works: Feudal Society (1939–40); contextual reception study: Susan W. Friedman, Marc Bloch, Sociology and Geography

after.scope_note: Durkheim and selected collaborators, recipients and interlocutors, not a membership register. Collective explanation does not imply that all institutions are useful or all differentiation creates solidarity. Colonial-era categories and ethnographic generalizations remain claims to assess. Bloch’s engagement is selective; modernization and Bourdieu links still need more precise reception passages.

strands.title: Social facts and institutional resistance
strands.focus: Durkheim’s examples include obligations, signs and monetary practices. Externality and coercive capacity distinguish his object; mere statistical commonness does not suffice.

strands.title: Origins, functions and critical antecedents
strands.focus: Chapter V disputes Comte’s and Spencer’s utility-based explanations: identifying a use does not explain an institution’s origin, and functions can change.

strands.title: Differentiation and failures of solidarity
strands.focus: Division of labor can produce conflict and anomie. Durkheim’s discussion of crises and capital/labor antagonism qualifies any automatic equation of differentiation with cohesion.
strands.works: Division of Labour (1893), book III chapter I

strands.title: Religious life and collective categories
strands.focus: Sacred practices and collective membership are distinguished from a purely private belief. The proposed social formation of categories is an argument to assess, not an established origin of all thought.
strands.works: Elementary Forms (1912), introduction and religion definition

strands.title: Sacrifice, participants and mediation
strands.focus: Hubert and Mauss build on and revise earlier comparative scholarship. Their provisional model distinguishes ritual participants and movement between sacred and profane.
strands.works: “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899)

strands.title: Historical evidence and social science
strands.focus: Simiand’s methodological challenge and Bloch’s selective historical reception are different forms of engagement; Annales’ later reprint makes one continuing exchange explicit.
strands.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903; reprinted 1960); Bloch reception in Sociology and Geography

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering and language
strands.focus: Halbwachs’s memory inquiry and Meillet’s semantic history develop different objects from social relations. Shared vocabulary alone does not establish identical methods.
strands.works: Les Cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); “Comment les mots changent de sens” (1906)

added.relationship: Meillet explicitly applies Durkheim’s social-fact definition to language
added.evidence_note: The opening of the 1906 essay names Durkheim and applies externality and coercion to language; later passages examine social groups and semantic change. The target represents a broader linguistic context, not Saussure alone. No direct Durkheim-to-Saussure borrowing is established.
added.map_label: Meillet: language as a social fact

added.relationship: Hubert and Mauss acknowledge and revise comparative theories of sacrifice
added.evidence_note: Their essay’s introduction explicitly credits Tylor, Robertson Smith and Frazer while proposing a different, provisional account. This names antecedent resources within the wider Durkheimian group, not the origin of Durkheim’s entire sociology. It differs from the reverse Radcliffe-Brown reception in edge_432.

before.evidence_note: Barthes adapts a theory of signs to cultural analysis; his later work changes its premises.

after.relationship: Barthes adapts linguistic distinctions and proposes reversing the semiology hierarchy
after.evidence_note: Elements of Semiology introduction explicitly invokes the Course but proposes making semiology part of linguistics. The categories are a provisional research programme, not an unchanged transfer or a summary of Barthes’s later work.

before.evidence_note: Lacan reworks signifier/signified relations; this does not make his account identical to Saussure’s.

after.relationship: Lacan adapts linguistic resources in his account of the Symbolic
after.evidence_note: The SEP historical account and section 2.1.2 distinguish signifying chains, langage from particular langues, and later revisions. This is scholarly secondary reception evidence; Lacan’s primary transformation of the sign diagram remains to be checked.

before.relationship: questions the privileging of speech and stable signifieds
before.evidence_note: The critique addresses the hierarchy of speech/writing and assumptions of presence; not the rejection of all linguistics.

after.relationship: Derrida questions the speech/writing hierarchy while working through differential relations
after.evidence_note: The consulted chapter 2 excerpt examines Saussure’s phonological foundations and develops the trace through difference. It is neither rejection of every linguistic insight nor a claim that Saussure simply assigns a fixed meaning to each word. English edition metadata remains unresolved.

before.relationship: social facts and collective representations are adapted
before.evidence_note: Bloch’s acknowledgement of Durkheim supports an intellectual debt. The adaptation is selective; Annales is neither identical to Durkheimian sociology nor uniform across its historians.

after.relationship: Bloch’s selective reception and Simiand’s methodological intervention connect sociology with Annales
after.evidence_note: The existing Bloch acknowledgment supports a qualified intellectual debt. Annales’ 1960 editors explicitly reprint Simiand’s 1903 essay to sustain their dialogue with social science. These are distinct reception examples, not evidence that every Annales historian follows Durkheim.

before.relationship: differentiation and solidarity enter later social theory
before.evidence_note: Differentiation is a conceptual resource in later social theory; direct transmission to particular modernization theorists needs a more specific reference.

after.relationship: Differentiation and solidarity provide a proposed resource for later social theory
after.evidence_note: Durkheim’s book III explicitly discusses failures of solidarity, qualifying a simple modernization story. This primary passage supports the conceptual distinction but does not establish direct reception by a particular modernization theorist; the existing generic reference remains insufficient for that transmission.

before.relationship: supplies a theory of relational signs adapted and contested in later historical debates
before.evidence_note: Spiegel explicitly traces a route from structural linguistics to the linguistic turn; this summary edge does not replace the distinct intermediaries. Relational signs are a resource later adapted and challenged; structuralism and poststructuralism are not identical.

after.relationship: Relational signs become a resource disputed in historical debates
after.evidence_note: Spiegel’s 2009 retrospective opening and notes 1–3 document a named account of this reception and disagreements about reference. Her summary is not a neutral statement of all Saussure’s claims; she also distinguishes the analytic-philosophy route associated with Rorty.

before.relationship: Radcliffe-Brown explicitly adapts Durkheim’s account of function
before.evidence_note: The indexed 1935 primary excerpt credits Durkheim and modifies the language of needs to avoid teleology. This is a named conceptual borrowing, not an origin for the entire discipline.

after.relationship: Radcliffe-Brown explicitly adapts Durkheim’s account of function
after.evidence_note: The indexed 1935 primary excerpt credits Durkheim and modifies the language of needs to avoid teleology. This is a named conceptual borrowing, not an origin for the entire discipline. Durkheim’s own Rules chapter V distinguishes causal origins from functions and rejects explanation by utility alone.

added.title: Ferdinand de Saussure, Cours de linguistique générale (1916), edited by Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye with Albert Riedlinger; consulted Payot edition, 1971.
added.citation: Ferdinand de Saussure, Cours de linguistique générale (1916), edited by Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye with Albert Riedlinger; consulted Payot edition, 1971.

verification.note: Wikisource transcription: first-edition preface, Part I chapters I–III selected passages, and Part II chapter IV on value read. Preface distinguishes the three lecture courses, student notebooks, editorial collation and reconstruction; the preceding R. L. Wagner text dated 1948 is not the original preface. Part I treats arbitrariness, social inheritance, time and two analytical axes; Part II distinguishes value from isolated signification. The consulted printing is 1971, not the 1916 first printing. Manuscripts and later critical editions not compared. Chapter pages are linked from this contents page.

added.citation: Antoine Meillet, “Comment les mots changent de sens,” L’Année sociologique 9 (1904–1905), published 1906, 6–43.

verification.note: Primary section I opening and selected discussion of social groups, occupational vocabularies, borrowing and semantic change read. Meillet explicitly applies Durkheim’s externality/coercion definition to language. This documents Meillet’s reception, not direct Durkheim influence on Saussure. His introductory equation of languages with nations is a historical assumption, not adopted as a general description of multilingual societies. Individual etymologies not independently checked.

added.citation: Roland Barthes, Éléments de sémiologie (1964); Elements of Semiology, linked English excerpt identifies Hill and Wang, 1968.

verification.note: Primary introduction and sections I.1.1–I.1.8 and I.2.1 read. Barthes proposes adapting linguistic distinctions and reversing Saussure’s linguistics/semiology hierarchy; he describes Hjelmslev’s schema, norm and usage and treats transfers as provisional. The webpage reproduces only the first half. Its speculation about a Durkheim–Saussure transmission is not evidence establishing that transmission. Original French journal record: https://www.persee.fr/doc/comm_0588-8018_1964_num_4_1_1029 .

added.citation: Jacques Derrida, De la grammatologie (1967), chapter 2, “Linguistics and Grammatology”; linked English excerpt.

added.citation: Émile Durkheim, Les Règles de la méthode sociologique (1895); consulted Alcan edition, 1919, chapters I and V.

verification.note: Primary chapter I opening and later definition passages, and chapter V opening read in the linked Wikisource chapters. Social facts include signs, obligations and institutions with externality and resistance; common occurrence alone is insufficient. Chapter V explicitly criticizes Comte and Spencer for conflating utility with origins and distinguishes causes from functions, including survivals and changed uses. The later printing is identified; no complete comparative-method or original-edition collation claimed.

Durkheim discusses crises and capital/labor antagonism as failures of solidarity; differentiation does not guarantee integration. The normal/pathological vocabulary and his historical examples are his claims, not independently verified conclusions. Full book and chapter on forced division remain unread here.

added.citation: Émile Durkheim, Les Formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse (1912); The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life, translated by Joseph Ward Swain (1915).

verification.note: Primary selected introduction pp. 9–19, religion definition pp. 46–47, and conclusion IV on categories read in Gutenberg transcription. Supports the proposed social formation of categories and collective practices around sacred things. Durkheim presents a sociological alternative to individual empiricism and unexplained apriorism. Australian ethnographic evidence and claims about earliest religion are not independently established by these readings; the book is not treated as a current ethnographic authority.

Remaining pages, including the famous three-idols passage, not read here; editorial reception is not attributed to Simiand himself.

after.title: Gabrielle M. Spiegel, “The Task of the Historian” (2009): retrospective on the linguistic turn

verification.note: AHA primary presidential address opening on the linguistic turn and notes 1–3 read. Spiegel retrospectively traces a Saussurean route and records disputes over realism and reference; this is evidence of historiographical reception, not a neutral synopsis of Saussure or an exclusive origin story. Note 3 distinguishes the analytic-philosophy route through Rorty. Full address not reviewed here.

saussure.people: Roster grows from two to nine: Bally, Sechehaye and Riedlinger make editorial mediation explicit; Meillet, Trubetzkoy and Hjelmslev differentiate programmes; Spiegel supplies a retrospective historical reception. Jakobson gains a distinct argument beyond mediation to Lévi-Strauss. Benveniste and wider linguistic traditions remain gaps, not silently claimed coverage.
saussure.works_and_arguments: Read the Course preface and selected conceptual chapters; specify value, signification, arbitrariness and language states/change. Meillet’s social semantics and Jakobson’s selection/combination are distinguished. Hjelmslev’s original-issue dating and the reprint metadata are explicitly limited. No baseline empty works here.
saussure.internal_distinctions: Eight editorial approaches separate publication, value, time, social semantics, phonology, schema/usage, selection/combination and later reception. These overlap and are not exclusive school memberships.
saussure.incoming_connections: Meillet’s explicit application of Durkheim provides a named incoming contribution through the broader linguistic entry; it does not prove Durkheim influenced Saussure. Student notes and editorial labor supply another kind of intellectual mediation, represented in the roster without invented full nodes. Derrida’s incoming critique gains a primary excerpt; the Foucault comparison remains undirected.
saussure.outgoing_connections: Preserve newly checked Lévi-Strauss phonological reception. Specify Barthes’s proposed inversion of the semiology hierarchy; upgrade scoped secondary Lacan support and Spiegel’s retrospective historical reception. Neither Lacan nor all linguistic-turn historians simply reproduce the Course.
saussure.evidence_and_interpretation: Eleven new sources across the batch and two existing-source upgrades distinguish original arguments, later editions, reception and bibliography. Meillet’s national assumptions are not adopted. The 1971 Course printing and its embedded 1948 Wagner passage are distinguished from the first-edition preface. Derrida’s excerpt has unreliable English edition metadata; Hjelmslev’s issue/bibliography dates remain explicit.

durkheim.people: Roster grows from one to seven, differentiating Hubert and Mauss’s collaboration, Simiand’s methodological inquiry, Halbwachs’s memory project, Meillet’s social linguistics and Bloch’s selective historical reception. This is not a membership register; Hertz, Bouglé and other interlocutors remain coverage gaps.
durkheim.works_and_arguments: Rules chapter I identifies externality/resistance; chapter V distinguishes causes/functions and criticizes Comte/Spencer’s utility explanations. Division book III checks failures of solidarity. Elementary Forms supplies religion and collective-category arguments. Hubert/Mauss’s introduction and mediation passages provide a specific collaborative project. Simiand’s 1903 opening and 1960 editorial reception are separately attributed.
durkheim.internal_distinctions: Seven approaches distinguish social facts, causes/functions, failures of solidarity, religious categories, sacrifice, historical method and memory/language applications. Normal/pathological and early-religion claims remain historical propositions rather than accepted empirical descriptions.
durkheim.incoming_connections: New incoming contribution names the comparative resources Hubert/Mauss acknowledge in Tylor, Robertson Smith and Frazer. Rules directly engages Comte and Spencer; Elementary Forms positions social categories against empiricism/apriorism. These critical resources are described without inventing a universal sociology origin edge.
durkheim.outgoing_connections: Add Meillet’s documented social-fact reception; strengthen Annales with its editors’ explicit 1960 Simiand reprint. Preserve distinct Lévi-Strauss/Mauss and Radcliffe-Brown routes. Clarify differentiation without claiming primary Durkheim evidence proves modernization reception. Halbwachs’s formation and Bourdieu’s classification reception remain specifically scoped gaps.
durkheim.evidence_and_interpretation: Later French and English editions are identified. Primary propositions do not validate colonial-era examples. The Bourdieu Persée record exposes only page 405, and the attempted PDF endpoint failed; no claim to reading the requisite 406–408 passages. Bloch’s source remains a publisher-indexed scholarly introduction, with an additional publisher PDF located but screenshot retrieval unsuccessful.

saussure: Check Benveniste’s 1939 “Nature du signe linguistique” and a specific historical-institutional semantics work; distinguish his criticism from wholesale rejection of Saussure, then assess additional linguistic traditions against this teaching scope.

Resolve Hjelmslev’s 1942 issue versus 1943 bibliography date from the original colophon, and identify the Jakobson reprint’s original publication/edition from a publisher or title page; retain current explicit limits until then.

Obtain Lacan’s primary passage transforming the sign diagram and a reliable edition of Derrida’s chapter 2; current support is respectively scoped SEP exposition and an English excerpt with uncorroborated 1974 heading.
Compare at least one original Saussure lecture notebook or critical edition against the reconstructed Course before attributing particular editorial formulations directly to a delivered lecture.
durkheim: Obtain Bourdieu “Sur le pouvoir symbolique” (1977), pp. 406–408, for the precise Durkheim and Saussure reception; Persée page 405 was readable but the direct PDF endpoint failed. Preserve edge_178’s limitation meanwhile.

Check a named modernization theorist’s direct discussion of Durkheim, and Halbwachs’s intellectual formation; Durkheim’s own differentiation argument and later memory reception do not establish these transmission steps.
Assess Hertz, Bouglé and critiques of Primitive Classification with primary or substantive scholarly support; do not treat Elementary Forms as validation of colonial-era ethnographic generalizations.
Read further Simiand 1903 pages and Bloch’s quoted 1931 statement in context during the Annales batch; the 1960 reprint note and Friedman’s indexed introduction establish narrower reception claims.
